entityDossier.whatItIs: The DoD Special Access Program Central Office (SAPCO) and the governance stack built around it — the Special Access Program Oversight Committee (SAPOC), the Senior Review Group (SRG), the SAP Senior Working Group (SSWG), and the Cognizant Authority SAPCOs inside each Component — is the machinery that creates, names, compartments, funds, audits and reports every DoD Special Access Program. It is defined by DoD Directive 5205.07, DoD Instruction 5205.11 (12 September 2024), and DoD Manual 5205.07 (17 January 2025). The Director, DoD SAPCO sits directly under the Deputy Secretary of Defense and is the Department's single point of congressional liaison for SAPs.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: If a legacy recovery and reverse-engineering effort has been carried inside the Department of Defense since the 1940s, this is the architecture that would hold it, and this is the architecture that would keep Congress from seeing it. DoDI 5205.11 states in plain text that the Secretary of Defense may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as 'waived' when standard congressional reporting 'would adversely affect national security' — a category whose existence is admitted, whose contents are not. The same office that decides what is waived is the office through which every congressional inquiry about SAPs must pass; it is simultaneously the gatekeeper and the answering service. Chairwoman Anna Paulina Luna reported in September 2025 that DoD told Oversight Committee staff that only HASC and HAC-D members could be read into UAP-relevant SAP material at all, meaning the committee actually investigating concealment was structurally locked out by the concealment architecture. And Congress's own annual SAP report requirement under 10 U.S.C. 119(a)-(b) terminated by operation of law on 31 December 2021 — the year before AARO was stood up.
entityDossier.narrative:
The Special Access Program is the American government's designed answer to a question nobody asked out loud: how do you run a program that no one is allowed to know exists, and still call it lawful? The answer is a tiered architecture with a central clearinghouse, and that clearinghouse is the DoD Special Access Program Central Office.

The structure is documented, and the documentation is more revealing than any leak. DoD Instruction 5205.11, reissued 12 September 2024, assigns oversight authority over DoD SAPs to four Principal Staff Assistants: the Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering, the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment, the Under Secretary of Defense for Policy, and the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security. Those four offices map with uncomfortable precision onto the four functions a recovery-and-exploitation effort would require: science, procurement, policy cover, and security. Below them sit Cognizant Authority SAPCOs inside each Component, each with its own security director, access approval authority, and classification guide annexes.

Above them sits the Director, DoD SAPCO, who under DoDM 5205.07 operates 'Under the authority, direction, and control of the Deputy Secretary of Defense' — not the Secretary, not the Under Secretary for Intelligence and Security, but the Deputy. That reporting line matters. It means SAP governance runs through the Department's chief operating officer, the official who signs the memoranda establishing and terminating programs, and the official who convenes the SAPOC and the SRG. The Deputy Secretary is the single human node through which the entire waived-program universe passes.

The most quotable sentence in the entire corpus is DoDI 5205.11's own description of waiver: 'The Secretary of Defense may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as "waived" when it is determined that using standard procedures for reporting to Congress would adversely affect national security, pursuant to Section 119 of Title 10, United States Code. Waived SAPs remain subject to congressional oversight.' The second sentence is the tell. It is an assertion of a conclusion, not a description of a mechanism. The mechanism is in 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2): when the Secretary waives, the information and the justification go 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' Subsection (g) defines the defense committees as the Armed Services and Appropriations committees of both chambers plus their defense subcommittees. Chairman plus ranking member of six bodies equals twelve members of Congress — for the most sensitive programs in the Department, out of 535.

That is the theory. In practice it is worse. The termination note attached to 10 U.S.C. 119 records that the annual SAP report to the defense committees under subsections (a) and (b) — the report enumerating every SAP, its cost history and its milestones — was terminated effective 31 December 2021 by section 1061 of Public Law 114-328. The single most comprehensive recurring window Congress had into the SAP portfolio closed by statute the year before the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office was created, and eleven months before the Intelligence Authorization Act rewrote 50 U.S.C. 3373 to demand a historical accounting of exactly the sort of program that report would have listed.

The SAPOC's annual review, per DoDI 5205.11, expressly includes assessment of 'All waived DoD SAPs to determine the need for continued waived status.' Somebody, once a year, reads a list of the programs Congress is not told about and decides whether to keep not telling Congress. That list exists. It has a custodian. Its custodian answers to the Deputy Secretary of Defense.

Two further mechanisms deserve analyst attention. First, 'carve out': DoDI 5205.11 authorizes Component heads to initiate actions replacing Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency security cognizance at contractor facilities, and to notify DCSA that it is 'relieved from inspection authority.' Carve-out removes the government's default industrial-security inspector from a contractor site. Whatever is inside a carved-out facility is inspected only by the program's own security apparatus. Second, the DoD SAPCO 'Functions as the DoD single point of congressional liaison concerning SAPs' and verifies that congressional offices approved to store SAP information implement DoD's own security requirements — meaning the Department also sets the terms on which the legislature may hold what the Department gives it.

Representative Eric Burlison's 22 May 2026 interrogatories to MITRE attack this architecture directly. He asks MITRE to identify every SAP, Controlled Access Program, Alternative Compensatory Control Measure, Managed-Need-To-Know codeword, DOE Restricted Data compartment and SIGMA category it touched in connection with UAP records, and for each one to state 'whether the program was reported to the appropriate congressional committees.' That question only has to be asked if the answer might be no.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The congressional oversight apparatus for the legacy program question spans four venues with mismatched authorities: the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform (broad jurisdiction, no SAP access), the House and Senate Armed Services and Appropriations committees (SAP access, narrow appetite), the two intelligence committees (Controlled Access Program access), and the twelve-member chairman-and-ranking-member channel through which waived Special Access Programs are reported under 10 U.S.C. 119(e). Since 2021 Congress has legislated repeatedly and specifically against concealment, and has been told, repeatedly and specifically, that there is nothing to conceal.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: Congress is not a bystander in this record; it is the party that wrote into permanent law the demand that the Executive account for 'any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress.' That sentence exists in the United States Code because members with access to classified briefings concluded such programs might exist. Congress then legislated that AARO must enumerate every instance in which data was withheld from it on classification grounds, barred contractors from charging UAP-related independent research and development to overhead unless the material is furnished to Congress, and created a statutory UAP Records Collection at the National Archives. Each of those provisions is a countermeasure, and countermeasures are designed against something. What Congress has not obtained is compliance: the eminent-domain and Review Board provisions were stripped in conference, the annual SAP report requirement lapsed on 31 December 2021, and in September 2025 the chairwoman of the investigating task force told the public that DoD would not read her members in at all.
entityDossier.narrative:
Congressional oversight of the legacy program problem has a structural defect that no amount of legislative will has cured: the committees with the appetite lack the access, and the committees with the access lack the appetite.

The modern sequence begins on 26 July 2023, when the House Oversight Committee's National Security subcommittee convened 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Implications on National Security, Public Safety, and Government Transparency.' Former National Reconnaissance Office and National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency officer David Grusch testified under oath alongside former Navy pilot Ryan Graves and retired Navy Commander David Fravor. Grusch alleged a decades-long crash-retrieval and reverse-engineering effort, recovery of non-human biologics, and misappropriation of funds to evade congressional oversight, and said the specifics required a classified setting. The hearing produced a printed transcript, a legislative wave, and no records.

The legislative wave crested in the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act. Senators Chuck Schumer and Mike Rounds had drafted the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act, which passed the Senate with three teeth: a presidentially appointed nine-member Review Board, a Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan, and federal eminent domain over recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence held by private parties. Conference removed all three. What survived became sections 1841 through 1843 of Public Law 118-31, codified at 44 U.S.C. 2107 note: a UAP Records Collection at the National Archives, populated by 'copies of all Government, Government-provided, or Government-funded records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena, technologies of unknown origin, and non-human intelligence,' housed by NARA in Record Group 615. The eminent domain provision — the only clause that would have compelled a private contractor to surrender physical material — was the one the private contractors did not have to face.

What survived elsewhere in the same law is less discussed and arguably sharper. Section 1687(b) of P.L. 118-31 provides that, consistent with DoDI 3204.01, 'independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses' on covered contracts 'unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership.' Congress legislated, in the FY2024 NDAA, against a specific accounting mechanism by which a defense contractor could fund UAP work with taxpayer money routed through overhead and owe nobody an explanation. That provision is a fingerprint.

The permanent statute carries more. 50 U.S.C. 3373(l)(4) requires the AARO Director, every briefing period, to give the chairs and ranking members of the Armed Services and Intelligence committees 'an enumeration of any instances in which data relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena was not provided to the Office because of classification restrictions on that data or for any other reason.' Congress anticipated that its own office would be stonewalled by other parts of the Executive and built a tripwire. Section 3373(j) requires the Historical Record Report to reach back to 1 January 1945 and to itemize 'any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress,' together with 'any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information.' The Comptroller General was directed by section 6803 of P.L. 117-263 to audit that very report process with cleared GAO personnel and to brief Congress semiannually on it.

Congress kept legislating. Public Law 119-60, enacted 18 December 2025, amended 50 U.S.C. 3373(f)(1)(A) so that the data-sharing mandate binds every component of the Department of Defense, not merely elements of the intelligence community — an amendment that would be pointless unless DoD components had been withholding under the old text. The same act added subsection (l)(5), requiring briefings to include details of NORAD and USNORTHCOM intercepts of UAP, with the first post-enactment briefing to reach back to 1 January 2004. Section 1673(a) ordered the AARO Director to make, within 180 days, 'an accounting of security classification guides that apply to information used for reports and investigations of unidentified anomalous phenomena.' Congress is now demanding an inventory of the classification instruments themselves.

Against all of this stands the access problem. On 11 February 2025 Chairman James Comer created the Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets under Rep. Anna Paulina Luna, authorized for six months under Committee Rules. On 9 September 2025 Luna told the public that DoD had informed her staff that only HASC and HAC-D members could be read into the relevant SAPs, and that any other Member required the approval of the chairman and ranking member of both. She added: 'Independent SAP oversight has presented a consistent problem for Congress as the program's budgets are classified.' That is the architecture of 10 U.S.C. 119 operating exactly as designed, against the committee investigating it.

entityDossier.whatItIs: Section 1683 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2022, Public Law 117-81, enacted 27 December 2021 at 135 Stat. 2118, is the statute that created the office lineage running from the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force through the Airborne Object Identification and Management Synchronization Group to the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office. It is codified at 50 U.S.C. 3373 and was rewritten wholesale a year later by section 6802(a) of the Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2023 (Public Law 117-263), and amended again in 2023 and 2025.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: This is the only place in the United States Code where Congress wrote down, in operative statutory language, that programs concerning unidentified anomalous phenomena may have been 'protected by restricted access' and 'not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress,' and demanded an accounting of them going back to 1 January 1945. It is also the only statute that directs the Secretary of Defense to designate line organizations for 'the testing of materials, medical studies, and development of theoretical models' relating to UAP, and to run a science plan whose stated purpose includes providing 'the foundation for potential future investments to replicate' anomalous performance characteristics. Congress did not merely authorize a reporting office; it authorized materials testing, medical study of exposed personnel, and replication research — the exact functional description of a reverse-engineering enterprise — and then required that any prior version of the same enterprise be disclosed. The statute's subsequent amendment history is a record of the Executive branch failing to comply.
entityDossier.narrative:
Section 1683 began as a modest reorganization and became, through two rewrites, the sharpest disclosure instrument in federal law. Read it as a chronology of what Congress learned.

The original enactment on 27 December 2021 stood up an office to absorb the Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Task Force, in the wake of the June 2021 ODNI preliminary assessment. A year later, section 6802(a) of the Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2023 amended the section generally — replacing it in full — and section 1673(c)(1) of the same law substituted 'anomalous' for 'aerial' wherever the word appeared. That single-word substitution is not cosmetic. It extended the statute's reach from aircraft to transmedium objects and submerged objects, a definitional move that matters if what is at issue includes things recovered from water.

The rewritten statute names the office the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office and hardwires a dual chain of command. The Director is appointed by the Secretary of Defense in consultation with the DNI; the Deputy Director is appointed by the DNI in coordination with the Secretary. The Director reports directly to the Deputy Secretary of Defense and the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence — and, separately, 'to the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security on all administrative matters.' That administrative reporting line runs to the same office that is a SAP Oversight Authority under DoDI 5205.11 and the DoD interface to the DNI's Controlled Access Program Central Office. The office chartered to find concealed compartments is administratively subordinate, in part, to the office that manages compartments.

Subsection (j) is the load-bearing clause. Within 540 days of 23 December 2022, the Director was to deliver to the defense committees, the intelligence committees and congressional leadership a written report on 'the historical record of the United States Government relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena,' drawn from intelligence community records, oral history interviews, open source analysis, interviews of current and former officials, and classified and unclassified national archives. It must focus on the period beginning 1 January 1945. And it must include 'a compilation and itemization of the key historical record of the involvement of the intelligence community with unidentified anomalous phenomena, including — (I) any program or activity that was protected by restricted access that has not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress; (II) successful or unsuccessful efforts to identify and track unidentified anomalous phenomena; and (III) any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect unclassified or classified information about unidentified anomalous phenomena or related activities.' Subsection (j)(2) obliges the Archivist of the United States to make classified NARA holdings available to the office for that purpose.

Subsections (e) and (g) are where the statute stops sounding like transparency legislation and starts sounding like a program charter. Under (e)(1), the Secretary of Defense in coordination with the DNI 'shall designate one or more line organizations that will be primarily responsible for scientific, technical, and operational analysis of data gathered by field investigations... including with respect to the testing of materials, medical studies, and development of theoretical models.' Under (e)(2), both officials must issue directives ensuring those line organizations 'has authority to draw on the special expertise of persons outside the Federal Government with appropriate security clearances.' Under (g), the science plan must account for performance 'that exceed the known state of the art in science or technology, including in the areas of propulsion, aerodynamic control, signatures, structures, materials, sensors, countermeasures, weapons, electronics, and power generation,' and 'provide the foundation for potential future investments to replicate or otherwise better understand any such advanced characteristics and performance.' Congress wrote replication into the law. Subsection (k)(1)(B)(xi) then requires each annual report to include 'An update on any efforts underway on the ability to capture or exploit discovered unidentified anomalous phenomena.'

Definitions matter here too. Subsection (n)(6) defines 'line organization' to exclude any component of the Office of the Secretary of Defense — pushing materials testing and medical studies out to service laboratories, agencies and national laboratories, and therefore out to contractor-operated facilities. Subsection (n)(7) defines transmedium objects as those observed transitioning between space and atmosphere, or atmosphere and water.

The amendment history is the compliance record. In December 2023, P.L. 118-31 §7341 moved the annual report obligation from the DNI and SecDef jointly onto the AARO Director alone. In December 2025, P.L. 119-60 §1672(b) rewrote subsection (f)(1)(A) so the data-availability mandate binds 'each element of the intelligence community and component of the Department of Defense' — the prior text covered only IC elements. Congress had to amend the statute to reach the Department of Defense's own components. Section 1671 added the NORAD/NORTHCOM intercept requirement with a 2004 lookback, and section 1673(a) demanded an accounting of the security classification guides themselves. Each amendment closes a door someone had walked through.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The NASA Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Independent Study Team was a 16-member external panel convened by NASA in 2022 under the Earth Science Advisory Committee, chaired by astrophysicist David Spergel of the Simons Foundation, with Dr. Daniel Evans of NASA Headquarters as Designated Federal Official. It held a single public meeting on 31 May 2023 and delivered its final report on 14 September 2023. On the same day NASA created a Director of UAP Research position and initially declined to name the appointee.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: The panel is a study in the shape of a hole. It was chartered to advise NASA on UAP using only unclassified civilian, commercial and open-source data, and it says so plainly — which means the one body assembled to bring scientific rigor to the question was structurally barred from the classified holdings where the question actually lives. Its report says the quiet part in print: military and intelligence sensor data are classified 'often because of what the imagery could reveal about U.S. technical capabilities to our adversaries, and not because of what is actually in the images,' and that these classified observations 'enhance the sense of mystery and conspiracy surrounding UAP, and they present an obstacle to scientific inquiry.' That is a federally chartered panel, in an official NASA publication, stating that classification is generating the appearance of concealment. Three of its sixteen members came from commercial remote-sensing, space-hardware and private-equity defense firms — Maxar, Redwire and AE Industrial Partners — and two from the FAA, making the panel a map of who holds the civilian sensor data that would matter. And the harassment record around the panel and the withheld name of NASA's UAP research director are themselves artifacts: the cost of association was high enough that the agency initially treated the identity of a civil servant as a security matter.
entityDossier.narrative:
NASA's Independent Study Team was born of a specific institutional bet: that the agency with the most public trust and the least security baggage could drag UAP into normal science. The bet was placed by Administrator Bill Nelson and executed by the Science Mission Directorate under Nicola Fox, following her predecessor Thomas Zurbuchen, with the activity graciously hosted, in the report's own words, by NASA's Earth Science Division under the Earth Science Advisory Committee. That administrative placement is worth pausing on: a panel about unidentified objects in the airspace was parked in the division that studies the planet's surface and atmosphere. It kept the activity out of astrophysics and out of anything that would have implied a search for technology.

The roster reads as a deliberate coalition of civilian instrumentation. Chair David Spergel of the Simons Foundation. Anamaria Berea of George Mason, Federica Bianco of Delaware, Paula Bontempi of Rhode Island, Jennifer Buss of the Potomac Institute for Policy Studies, science journalist Nadia Drake, David Grinspoon of the Planetary Science Institute, retired astronaut Captain Scott Kelly, Matt Mountain of AURA, Joshua Semeter of Boston University, and Shelley Wright of UC San Diego. Then the operators: Warren Randolph and Karlin Toner from the Federal Aviation Administration, Walter Scott from Maxar Technologies, Mike Gold from Redwire Space, and Reggie Brothers from AE Industrial Partners. Two FAA officials, one commercial satellite imaging executive, one space infrastructure executive, and one defense-focused private equity operator who had previously been Under Secretary for Science and Technology at DHS. If the panel's recommendations pointed anywhere, they pointed at data these institutions own.

And they did. The report recommends NASA leverage its Earth-observing assets to probe local environmental conditions associated with UAP detected by other means, and 'explore enhancing collaborations with the U.S. commercial remote-sensing industry, which offer powerful constellations of high-resolution Earth-observing satellites.' It recommends multispectral and hyperspectral acquisition, AI and machine learning applied to anomaly detection, a crowdsourcing system built on open-source smartphone apps, and better leveraging of the Aviation Safety Reporting System, which NASA operates for the FAA, as 'a critical database for the whole-of-government effort.' Every one of those recommendations routes future UAP data through civilian and commercial channels rather than military ones. Read charitably, that is a strategy for building an evidentiary base outside the classification perimeter. Read uncharitably, it is a strategy for building an evidentiary base that will never intersect the classification perimeter.

The panel's own frustration surfaces in the passage that matters most. Discussing why existing observations cannot resolve UAP, the report states: 'In addition, much of the data collected by military sensors or intelligence satellites are classified—often because of what the imagery could reveal about U.S. technical capabilities to our adversaries, and not because of what is actually in the images. While essential for security, these classified observations enhance the sense of mystery and conspiracy surrounding UAP, and they present an obstacle to scientific inquiry.' A federal advisory panel wrote, in a public report, that the government's classification practice is manufacturing the appearance of a cover-up and blocking the science that would dispel it. That sentence is a finding about the concealment architecture, delivered by scientists who could not see inside it.

On the evidence question the report is careful and narrow: 'To date, in the peer-reviewed scientific literature, there is no conclusive evidence suggesting an extraterrestrial origin for UAP.' The qualifier is doing work — peer-reviewed literature is precisely the corpus from which classified holdings are absent. The panel also recorded that then-AARO Director Sean Kirkpatrick reported at its 31 May 2023 public meeting that AARO had collected more than 800 reported events, against 263 reports filed in the 17 years before March 2021.

The cost of participation is documented in the report itself: team members received hate mail from colleagues, were ridiculed and criticized on social media, and had firsthand knowledge of colleagues warned away from technosignature research on the grounds that it could damage scientific credibility and promotion prospects. On 14 September 2023 NASA announced the creation of a Director of UAP Research and Administrator Nelson said the identity would be withheld to prevent harassment. NASA reversed within hours and named Mark McInerney, a former NASA liaison to the Department of Defense on UAP matters. The reversal is instructive twice over: it shows the agency's first instinct was concealment framed as protection, and it shows how quickly that instinct collapsed under press pressure — which is not how the Department of Defense's instances of the same instinct have behaved.

The statutory tie is direct. 50 U.S.C. 3373(c)(6) requires AARO to coordinate with NASA, among other agencies. Burlison's 22 May 2026 MITRE interrogatories demand identification of all UAP-related work MITRE performed for or with NASA. NASA sits inside the legal architecture of the program question while its own expert panel sat outside the data.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The Task Force on the Declassification of Federal Secrets is a panel of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, established by Chairman James Comer on 11 February 2025 and chaired by Rep. Anna Paulina Luna (R-FL), authorized for six months under Committee Rules. Its announced portfolio spans the Kennedy, Robert Kennedy and King assassination records, UAP and USO, the Epstein files, COVID-19 origins and the 9/11 files. It has become the principal congressional venue for the legacy program question since 2025.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: This is the first congressional body to run at the concealment architecture rather than at the phenomenon. Its members subpoena-adjacent letters go to contractors and federally funded research and development centers rather than to the Pentagon press office, on the theory that the records are in private hands under federal sponsorship. Its chairwoman has stated on the record that the Department of Defense refused to read her members into the relevant special access programs, naming HASC and HAC-D as the only committees with access — which converts a suspicion about compartmentation into a documented, dated institutional fact. Its member Eric Burlison has converted that finding into legislative interrogatories to MIT Lincoln Laboratory and The MITRE Corporation demanding enumeration of SAPs, ACCMs, cover programs, hidden funding and instructions to avoid certain vocabulary. And its chairwoman has used her opening statement to attack the credibility of the former AARO director by name, making the government's own denial instrument a subject of the investigation.
entityDossier.narrative:
The Task Force exists because a different theory of the problem won an internal argument. For four years the congressional approach to UAP was to demand better reports from the Executive branch. The Task Force's approach is to demand records from whoever physically holds them, and to treat classification as a claim to be adjudicated rather than an answer to be accepted.

It was created on 11 February 2025 when Chairman James Comer announced the panel and named Rep. Anna Paulina Luna to lead it, following President Trump's 23 January 2025 executive order on declassification of records concerning the assassinations of President Kennedy, Senator Robert Kennedy and Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. Comer framed it in institution-repair language: 'This secrecy has sowed distrust in our institutions.' Luna's own statement laid out a portfolio nobody expected a single panel to carry: 'We will also investigate UAPs/USOs, the Epstein client list, COVID-19 origins, and the 9/11 files.' The Task Force was authorized for six months pursuant to Committee Rules, and Comer and Luna transmitted eleven letters the same day. Its first hearing addressed the JFK files; Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA) was initially the ranking member, and by the September 2025 UAP hearing Luna was yielding to Ranking Member Crockett.

The 9 September 2025 hearing, 'Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection,' is the panel's substantive turn. Four witnesses testified: Air Force veteran Jeffrey Nuccetelli, Chief Alexandro Wiggins, journalist George Knapp, and Air Force veteran Dylan Borland. Luna's opening statement is the single most useful congressional document on the access problem. She described following a lead from active-duty Air Force pilot whistleblowers alleging a cover-up of UAP activity at Eglin Air Force Base, pursued with former Rep. Matt Gaetz and Rep. Tim Burchett. She said pilots decline to come forward out of fear for their flight status and careers. And then she stated the mechanism: 'In preparation for previous UAP hearings, the Committee repeatedly asked DoD to allow Members to view videos and files relating to UAP incidents. Unfortunately, DoD notified Committee staff that due to the Department's special access program (SAP) rules, only members of the House Armed Services Committee (HASC) and the Defense Subcommittee of the House Appropriations Committee (HAC-D) were allowed to be "read in" on such programs. For a non-committee Member to be allowed to view these documents and videos, individual Members must be approved by the Chairman and Ranking Member of both HASC and HAC-D.' She added that 'Independent SAP oversight has presented a consistent problem for Congress as the program's budgets are classified.'

That is 10 U.S.C. 119 operating as designed, quoted from the receiving end by a committee chairwoman. It also identifies precisely four people — the chairs and ranking members of HASC and HAC-D — as the gatekeepers for any Oversight Committee member seeking access.

Luna also went after AARO directly, calling former director Sean Kirkpatrick 'a documented liar' and questioning 'what his purpose at AARO really was if it was not to follow up on investigations and disclose his findings to Members of Congress.' She entered into the record former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence Chris Mellon's characterization of an AARO report as 'the most error-ridden and unsatisfactory government report I can recall reading during or after decades of government service,' noting Mellon's claims that it was the first AARO report submitted to Congress without the DNI's sign-off, that it omitted agencies with known UAP investigations, and that it omitted any discussion of efforts to hide information — including at U.S. Customs and Border Protection. A congressional task force treating the government's own investigative office as a suspect witness is a meaningful shift in posture.

The Task Force's method matured into contractor-directed process in 2026. On 7 May 2026 Burlison wrote to MIT Lincoln Laboratory about a reel-to-reel recording catalogued as 'AF-ATIC-FILM, 03/52' from the Beacon Hill Study, labeled 'flying saucer talk,' with Edward J. Ruppelt as briefer. On 22 May 2026 he transmitted ten pages of legislative interrogatories to MITRE, copied to Luna, Comer, and Information Security Oversight Office Director Michael D. Thomas. Both letters run on the same statutory theory: sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 NDAA, codified at 44 U.S.C. 2107 note, create a UAP Records Collection at NARA in Record Group 615 that encompasses government-funded records, and contractor custody does not defeat it. Burlison's framing in the accompanying release is the Task Force's thesis in one sentence: FFRDCs 'cannot become private vaults for federal records.'

The backdrop by 2026 is a Trump administration declassification push. Following a 19 February 2026 Trump directive, the Department of War began publishing declassified UAP files in May 2026 under the banner PURSUE — Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters — at war.gov/ufo. Burlison's press release places his MITRE inquiry explicitly inside that effort, testing whether agencies, contractors, FFRDCs and laboratories are actually complying.

entityDossier.whatItIs: A ten-page package of legislative interrogatories and production requests dated 22 May 2026, sent by Rep. Eric Burlison (R-MO-07) to Dr. Mark Peters, President and Chief Executive Officer, and Christopher Land, Senior Vice President and General Counsel, of The MITRE Corporation at 7525 Colshire Drive, McLean, Virginia. Copied to Task Force Chairwoman Anna Paulina Luna, Oversight Chairman James Comer, and Michael D. Thomas, Director of the Information Security Oversight Office at NARA. The enclosure runs eleven numbered sections and more than forty specific requests, with a relevant time period beginning 1 January 1930.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: This is the first congressional instrument that treats a federally funded research and development center as a potential custodian of the legacy program's paper. It does not ask MITRE whether UAP are real. It asks MITRE which Special Access Programs, Controlled Access Programs, Alternative Compensatory Control Measures, Managed-Need-To-Know codewords, DOE Restricted Data compartments and SIGMA categories it participated in touching UAP subject matter, and for each one, 'whether the program was reported to the appropriate congressional committees.' It asks for any classification guide, nondisclosure agreement or sponsor communication that instructed MITRE personnel to avoid the words UAP, UFO, USO, crash retrieval, reverse engineering, technology of unknown origin or non-human intelligence in their records. It asks for funding routed through 'a cover program' whose 'public description differed materially from the responsive work performed,' and for funding MITRE understood to be 'hidden from, not briefed to, or not readily visible to ordinary sponsor budget channels.' And it names twelve companies by name. The letter is a map of the concealment hypothesis rendered as a document request.
entityDossier.narrative:
Burlison's MITRE package is the moment the congressional inquiry stopped asking the Pentagon and started asking the people who hold the Pentagon's files.

The premise is stated in the cover letter's second paragraph. MITRE operates multiple FFRDCs, and 'By design, FFRDCs often receive special access to government facilities, data, sponsor requirements, and sensitive technical information that ordinary private contractors may not receive. This special public-trust role makes records stewardship, sponsor accountability, and congressional visibility especially important.' The statutory hook is sections 1841-1843 of the FY2024 NDAA and NARA's Record Group 615: if government-funded UAP records sit in a contractor's archive, the statute reaches them, and MITRE's status as a nonprofit operator does not create a safe harbor. DefenseScoop reported that FFRDCs are largely shielded from public disclosure by FOIA exemptions, and that some officials have warned this lets them hold government information the public has a right to see.

The scope is deliberately enormous. 'Unless otherwise specified, the relevant time period is January 1, 1930, to the present.' MITRE was incorporated in 1958; the 1930 start date is a trap for inherited archives, telling MITRE that if it contends the request is overbroad for a legacy period it must 'identify the earliest date for which MITRE can search reliably, the reason older records cannot be searched, and the custodian or sponsor most likely to hold the older records.' The definition of 'UAP-related' extends to any record 'described, coded, compartmented, or euphemized as involving' UAP, UFO, USO, transmedium craft, advanced aerospace threat, technology of unknown origin, non-human intelligence, legacy crash retrieval, crash retrieval, reverse engineering, recovered vehicle, recovered material, biological material, 'or equivalent terms.' Euphemism is named as a category of evidence.

The deadlines are tight and sequenced. Within five business days, designate a vice-president-level officer to coordinate. Within ten business days, issue and confirm a written preservation hold covering 'restricted systems, air-gapped environments, classified repositories, personal workspaces used for official business, archived systems, email, collaboration platforms, backup media, contractor/subcontractor systems, and offsite storage.' Within fourteen days, contact the office to coordinate a classified briefing for Task Force Members and cleared Committee staff at 'the appropriate TS/SCI/SAP level.' Within thirty days, written answers plus a records-location index naming repositories, custodians, contract vehicles, sponsors, classification authorities and record schedules. Within forty-five days, production of all unclassified responsive records in native electronic format with complete metadata, plus a segregated classified annex and a privilege and classification log. The letter warns that 'False statements, concealment, alteration, destruction, or obstruction in connection with this inquiry may implicate federal law, including but not limited to 18 U.S.C. §§ 1001, 1505, 1512, 1519, and 2071.'

The eleven enclosure sections read as a taxonomy of how a program stays hidden. Section I demands an accounting of records destroyed, degaussed, sanitized, reclassified, moved to a restricted system or 'placed under sponsor control,' with the authority and the responsible personnel named. Section II demands identification of every contract, IDIQ, GWAC, BPA, OTA and CRADA under which MITRE touched UAP information, and every individual involved with 'their specific functions and duties' — and names AARO, the UAP Task Force, AATIP, AAWSAP, DIA, CIA, NSA, NRO, NGA, ONI, NRL, DARPA, IARPA and DOE laboratories, 'or any successor, predecessor, cover, compartment, or renamed activity.' Section II.6 asks whether MITRE 'provided cover' for another entity's UAP work.

Section III is the compartmentation audit already described. Section IV asks what MITRE has and has not sent to NARA under the UAP Records Collection. Section V asks for sensor work across radar, optical, infrared, acoustic and undersea domains, expressly including 'SOSUS/IUSS-related' systems and 'unidentified submerged objects.' Section VI asks about recovered anomalous materials, isotope ratios, chain of custody, metamaterials, propulsion and 'cognitive interface systems' — and, in VI.4, about 'biological material, biological samples, human physiological effects, medical monitoring, occupational exposure, anomalous injury, cognitive or neurological effects, or environmental hazards associated with UAP-related materials, objects, fields, occupants, or events,' with the careful caveat that the request 'seeks records and safety documentation only and does not presume the validity of any particular biological claim.' The word 'occupants' is doing a great deal of work in a congressional document.

Section VII asks for SCIFs, SAPFs, vaults and 'material-containment work.' Section VIII asks for internal disclosures, retaliation, and nondisclosure instruments 'beyond standard government-secrecy obligations' that restricted personnel from reporting to Congress, IGs, AARO, NARA or law enforcement. Section IX names Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon/RRTX, Boeing, General Dynamics, SAIC, Leidos, Battelle, The Aerospace Corporation, Booz Allen Hamilton, BAE Systems and Bigelow Aerospace or its successors. Section X goes at the money. Section XI demands a certified response signed by a responsible MITRE officer and counsel.

MITRE's answer, given to DefenseScoop on 27 May 2026, was custodial rather than responsive: 'If any relevant material is found, we will coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work to determine how to best provide any assets.' That is a statement that anything found goes back to the sponsor, not to Congress. A member of Burlison's staff told DefenseScoop the letter was informed by 'advice from many whistleblowers, disclosure advocacy organizations, and those working at FFRDCs.'

The MITRE package was not the first shot. On 7 May 2026 Burlison had written to MIT Lincoln Laboratory Director Melissa G. Choi and counsel David A. Suski about a single object: a reel-to-reel recording catalogued as 'AF-ATIC-FILM, 03/52' from the Beacon Hill Study, labeled 'flying saucer talk,' with Edward J. Ruppelt — then head of Project Blue Book — listed as the briefer. That letter demanded the laboratory determine whether the recording is extant, preserve it, digitize it to preservation grade, and transmit it with metadata to NARA for Record Group 615. It also instructed the laboratory to coordinate with the cognizant sponsor, the original classification authority, ISOO and the Public Interest Declassification Board if an active Security Classification Guide still applies to a 1952 tape.

entityDossier.denialPosture: MITRE has not denied holding responsive records. Its only public statement — that if relevant material is found it will 'coordinate with the federal agencies responsible for the work to determine how to best provide any assets' — asserts a custodial rather than a disclosing posture, positioning the sponsor agency, not Congress, as the recipient. That is precisely the routing Burlison's letter anticipated and attempted to foreclose by demanding that MITRE identify the sponsor, the classification authority and 'the shortest practical path to lawful disclosure to Congress and transfer to NARA.'
